text:
## 5.1 Clinical presentation 
Acute bronchiolitis typically presents with acute onset of upper respiratory prodrome of rhinitis or
congestion, low-grade fever and cough progressing to the symptoms of increasing respiratory distress
(tachypnoea and increased work of breathing) and wheezing (155, 164). Common signs include tachycardia,
tachypnoea, hyperinflated chest, hyperresonant sounds on chest percussion, wheezing and crackles. In
children with severe disease, there may be grunting, marked retractions, cyanosis or lethargy. Apnoea is
common in preterm babies and those aged less than 2months. The severity of bronchiolitis can vary from
mild symptoms to acute respiratory failure, but most cases are self-limiting and respond to symptomatic
care at home. Complications among the hospitalized may include severe respiratory distress or failure,
pneumothorax, myocardial injury, neutropenia, sepsis, shock and neurological complications (165, 166).

metadata.section: Summary of recommendations > 5.1 Clinical presentation

text:
## 5.2 Diagnosis and management 
The diagnosis and assessment of acute bronchiolitis is based on history and clinical examination.
Laboratory investigations, chest radiographs and virological studies are not routinely indicated (13, 164).
The majority of children can be managed at home with supportive care on an ambulatory basis. Home
care includes parental education about adequate feeding, nasal saline drops and the gentle suctioning
of nostrils to relieve nasal block, and early care-seeking in case of any worsening symptoms (13, 164). The
current practice for those hospitalized is supportive care, including humidified oxygen therapy, adequate
hydration and feeding, and close monitoring, with no specific interventions of proven benefit despite wide
variability in the acute bronchiolitis care (13, 164, 167). Children with severe respiratory distress may require
invasive mechanical ventilation, which is associated with various complications (ventilator-induced lung
injury, infection, airway trauma, vocal cord dysfunction and need for prolonged sedation) and significant
financial costs (168). However, various non-invasive modes of oxygen delivery are increasingly being used,
such as HFNC, CPAP, non-invasive positive pressure ventilation and bilevel positive airway pressure, which
may obviate the need for invasive mechanical ventilation and the complications related to it (169-173).

## 5.3 Scope and target audience 
This guideline reviews the current evidence on selected topics related to the diagnosis and management
of bronchiolitis in children aged less than 2years. It does not encompass all aspects of the management of
bronchiolitis, but discusses the priority clinical aspects for primary and secondary care levels, focusing on
controversial areas of clinical diagnosis and treatment, and addresses the following topic areas in detail:
clinical signs and symptoms for the diagnosis of bronchiolitis;
clinical indicators for admission;
the role of X-ray imaging in bronchiolitis;
oxygen therapy and delivery in the treatment of bronchiolitis; and
the use of nebulized normal saline in the treatment of bronchiolitis.
The prioritized PICO questions discussed in section 6 are outlined in Annex 2.
The target audience for these recommendations are policy-makers and health care professionals working
in diverse settings and with variable availability of resources, in particular those in LMICs.

text:
## 6.1 Clinical signs and symptoms for the diagnosis of bronchiolitis 
Guiding principle for using clinical symptoms and signs in supporting a probable
diagnosis of bronchiolitis in an infant or child
Good practice statement 1: In infants and children aged less than 2years presenting with
cough and difficulty in breathing, a comprehensive history and assessment of clinical signs
and symptoms should be done. A diagnosis of bronchiolitis can be suspected if they have a
history of a prodrome of an upper respiratory tract infection with rhinitis or coryza and cough,
followed by respiratory distress with a low-grade fever, and any presence of tachypnoea (fast
breathing), chest indrawing and diffuse wheeze or crackles on auscultation.
Assessment of clinical signs should include the IMCI (3) general danger signs,4 cyanosis,
respiratory rate, looking for chest indrawing, listening for a wheeze or crackles, and
measuring oxygen saturation.
Infants with viral bronchiolitis are usually not very ill looking, and many have a prolonged
expiratory phase of breathing associated with wheeze.
During an RSV outbreak, a higher index of suspicion should be maintained in the differential
diagnosis for infants presenting with respiratory symptoms.
A comprehensive history should also elicit presence of any risk factors and comorbidities,
such as prematurity, children who are immunocompromized, and children with asthma
or reactive airway disease, chronic lung disease, chronic neurological conditions or
congenital heart conditions, and breastfeeding status.
6.1.1 Summary of evidence
The systematic review identified six observational studies from five countries (Australia, India, Iran (Islamic
Republic of), Saudi Arabia and Viet Nam) with a total sample size of 1396 participants (174-179). Outcomes
of interest were correct diagnosis, sensitivity and specificity, and the appropriate use of antibiotics. None of
the studies looked at the diagnostic accuracy of the signs and symptoms or whether they were associated
with the appropriate use of antibiotics. All studies were assessed as having high risk of bias owing to study
design, some were retrospective with missing data, or had a low sample size of less than 100, or had
reporting concerns.

The most common symptoms and signs were cough (64%), difficulty in breathing (56%), tachypnoea
(52%), nasal discharge (52%), wheeze (51%), fever (48%) and auscultatory sounds (44%) (Table 2). The GDG
observed that these signs were identified in cases suspected to have a clinical diagnosis of bronchiolitis

Recommendations for the management of bronchiolitis in infants and young children
6.1.2 Justification
A systematic review identified only six observational studies of suspected cases of bronchiolitis, where the
diagnosis was not confirmed. The major factors that were likely to be predictive of bronchiolitis were cough,
nasal discharge, difficulty in breathing, fever, tachypnoea, wheeze and auscultatory sounds, which align
with current clinical practice. However, the GDG noted that these signs were identified in cases suspected
to have a clinical diagnosis of bronchiolitis, which is based on the very same signs and symptoms used
for the diagnosis. In this respect, the GDG determined that, although a recommendation was not feasible
based on the available evidence, a good practice statement could be made in line with the WHO handbook
for guideline development (15), which would help clinicians make a diagnosis. This statement would guide
clinicians in diagnosing bronchiolitis, since the reviewed signs and symptoms align with standard clinical
practice and the counterfactual would not make sense.
6.1.3 Implementation considerations
Implementation will require clinicians to take into consideration the following.
There is usually an overlap in the clinical presentation of viral bronchiolitis and bacterial pneumonia,
and sometimes both exist or bacterial pneumonia may follow a viral upper respiratory infection.
Differential diagnoses to be considered include viral or bacterial pneumonia, and other serious
conditions, such as cardiac failure, gastro-oesophageal reflux, foreign body, tuberculosis, etc.

Implementation will require clinicians to take into consideration the following.
There is usually an overlap in the clinical presentation of viral bronchiolitis and bacterial pneumonia,
and sometimes both exist or bacterial pneumonia may follow a viral upper respiratory infection.
Differential diagnoses to be considered include viral or bacterial pneumonia, and other serious
conditions, such as cardiac failure, gastro-oesophageal reflux, foreign body, tuberculosis, etc.
Assessment of clinical signs should include IMCI general danger signs,5 cyanosis, respiratory rate,
looking for chest indrawing, listening for a wheeze or crackles, and measuring oxygen saturation.
A child who has IMCI general danger signs, who looks very unwell, has a high fever (temperature
>38°C) or a fever persisting for 5days or more, or is very hypoxic should not be assumed to have viral
bronchiolitis alone.
6.1.4 Research gaps
There is a need for a properly powered study that looks at the diagnostic accuracy of the signs and
symptoms of bronchiolitis.
There is a need to determine the signs and symptoms of bronchiolitis that are associated with
appropriate use of antibiotics.
5 The IMCI general danger signs are: inability to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, experiencing convulsions and being lethargic
or unconscious.

Guiding principle for assessing infants and children with suspected bronchiolitis
Good practice statement 2: In infants and children aged less than 2 years presenting with
suspected bronchiolitis, clinicians should perform a comprehensive assessment for the
presence of risk factors and signs of severe disease.
Indications for admission include: signs of severe disease, which include IMCI general
danger signs (inability to breastfeed or drink, vomiting everything, convulsions and lethargy
or unconsciousness), high temperature of ≥38°C, central cyanosis or SpO2 <90%, severe
respiratory distress, apnoea or history of apnoea, and presence of risk factors for severe
disease, which include comorbidities,a prematurity and age <3 months.
The indications for admission found in the review are mostly similar to the current WHO
guideline recommendations for the admission of severe pneumonia (1).
Clinicians should avoid unwarranted admissions that may lead to exposure to nosocomial
infections and avoidable hospital care costs.
Local context should be taken into consideration, particularly the availability of follow-up
or its accessibility, including travelling distances for patients, for example.
The temperature threshold of ≥38°C in cases of suspected bronchiolitis is significant and
might be justification for admission or close observation.
Comorbidities to consider in the history include: congenital cardiac lesions, chronic lung
disease, cerebral palsy and neurological conditions.

text: ## 6.3 Use of chest X-ray in the clinical management of bronchiolitis

metadata.section: Summary of recommendations > 6.3 Use of chest X-ray in the clinical management of bronchiolitis

text:
## Recommendation 1 
In infants and children aged less than 2 years presenting or hospitalized with suspected
bronchiolitis, routine use of chest X-ray is not suggested for the initial diagnosis and
management of bronchiolitis.
Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence.
Chest X-ray for hospitalized infants and children with suspected bronchiolitis should only
be considered on a case-by-case basis; for example, in the following clinical situations:
if there is high suspicion for other alternate diagnosis or underlying cardiac or chronic
lung disease related to risk factors elicited on history or physical examination;
if a child fails to respond to treatment or persistent symptoms for more than 2 weeks
without improvement;
if there is suspected bacterial superinfection or recurrent episodes of pneumonia;
if there is severe respiratory distress or severe hypoxaemia requiring admission to
high care or intensive care;
where a complication, such as effusion or pneumothorax, may be suspected; for
example, when there are unilateral signs of severe dullness to percussion or absent
breath sounds.
Recommendations for the management of bronchiolitis in infants and young children

6.3.1 Justification
Bronchiolitis is primarily a clinical diagnosis based on history and physical examination findings, including
cough, wheezing, tachypnoea and respiratory distress. In most cases, the diagnosis can be made based on
these clinical features alone without the need for confirmatory imaging studies. Despite the heterogeneity
in the three studies (188-190), the outcomes were consistent that routine chest X-ray (CXR) has no clinical
value in typical bronchiolitis, increases the risk of unnecessary antibiotic use and escalates care costs.
Driven by these outcomes, along with the evidence that imaging is unlikely to change management
outcomes, the GDG decided against routine CXR for suspected bronchiolitis. Routine CXR typically has a
low diagnostic yield in children with bronchiolitis, particularly in those without signs of severe respiratory
distress or complications.
6.3.2 Summary of evidence
The systematic review identified two prospective studies and one retrospective study conducted in the
emergency departments of tertiary hospitals in three high-income countries, with a total of 1194 children
aged less than 2years with clinically diagnosed bronchiolitis (188-190). All the three studies reported on the
rates of antibiotic therapy in those that received CXR or change in management after CXR, and, in addition,
one prospective cohort study reported on the proportion of CXRs that were inconsistent with clinically
diagnosed bronchiolitis. The infants in the included studies had moderate to severe bronchiolitis, with a
median age of 2.2months. The studies had mostly low risk of bias, mainly driven study design (188-190).
The findings from the prospective cohort study suggest that 133 children with typical bronchiolitis would

The findings from the prospective cohort study suggest that 133 children with typical bronchiolitis would
have to undergo radiography to identify one CXR that is suggestive of an alternate diagnosis (190). In
addition, it showed that children were five times more likely to receive antibiotic therapy post CXR compared
to the intended management plan pre CXR. The other prospective study of 697 children evaluated the
relationship between CXR use and antibiotic prescribing. Antibiotic use was significantly higher among
those who received a CXR (31%, 108 out of 355) compared with those who did not (8.4%, 28 out of 342). The
crude OR was 4.9 (95% CI: 3.1–7.8) (189). The retrospective cohort study assessed 227 children hospitalized
for acute bronchiolitis who received a routine CXR and 35 (15.4%) children who received a second CXR
in the event of complications. The routine CXRs showed lung abnormalities, specifically distension and/
or bronchial wall thickening (62.4%), focal opacity (19.9%) or atelectasis (17.7%). Antibiotic treatment was
started in 29 children (12.5%) following use of first CXR (188).
Overall, the three studies suggest that CXR contributed to only partial alteration of treatment of infants
hospitalized for acute bronchiolitis, but increased the risk of unnecessary administration of antibiotics.
There was low-certainty evidence about the additional value of CXR in management of bronchiolitis in
infants aged less than 2years.
The GDG determined that there was trivial benefit from doing routine CXR in all suspected bronchiolitis
cases. There was low-certainty evidence that routine CXR was not useful in confirming the diagnosis of
bronchiolitis, and that it contributed only partially to alteration of treatment and leads to unnecessary
antibiotic use with no clear benefits to patients. The characteristic radiographic findings of bronchiolitis,
such as hyperinflation and peri bronchial cuffing, are nonspecific and do not reliably differentiate
bronchiolitis from other viral respiratory infections. Nevertheless, the GDG observed that CXR may be
beneficial in identifying complications and the promotion of the appropriate use of antibiotics.

The GDG judged the undesirable effect as small with very low certainty of evidence. The GDG observed
that doing CXR routinely could result in increased use of unnecessary antibiotics, with the likelihood of
antimicrobial resistance, and might delay treatment, especially in low-resource settings where X-rays are
not easily available at lower-level facilities. Routine CXR may also lead to unnecessary exposure to ionizing
radiation which carries potential risks, including an increased lifetime risk of cancer. In addition, routine
CXR for children with suspected bronchiolitis can lead to unnecessary health care utilization and diversion
of resources, overcrowding in emergency departments, increased costs and potential delays in diagnosis
and treatment.
Preferences, values and acceptability: The GDG determined that patients and their caregivers value
the main outcome that is being measured and, therefore, on balance, the GDG decided on probably no
important uncertainty or variability. However, because of the diverse settings and levels of experience
of staff, there may be different degrees of familiarity with clinical practice guidelines. Although patients
are likely to accept CXRs, acceptability by clinicians may vary depending on a clinician’s confidence and
knowledge of the patient’s overall clinical condition. Administrators may not want the additional cost of
routine X-rays.
Resources required: There was no systematic review of the resources required. However, the GDG
observed that the direct costs will be increased, including medical consultation and specialist referrals
for unnecessary CXR, which will increase the cost to families. In a cost analysis study of omitting CXR in
diagnosis of acute bronchiolitis in 2009, omission of routine CXR saved Canadian dollars 59 per patient,
primarily due to savings in X-rays and hospitalizations (191).
Equity: In low-resource settings, there may be long waiting list for CXRs and this might affect ability of
patients to receive proper care. The GDG felt that equity is probably reduced in these settings.
Feasibility: The GDG recognized that the feasibility of routine CXR is affected by the limited financial and
human resources in LMIC settings and the lack of capacity.
6.3.3 Implementation considerations
Implementation will require family engagement through effective communication regarding
the diagnosis and natural course of the illness. Caregivers should be informed that most cases of
bronchiolitis resolve without the need for tests or medications, and that a CXR is unlikely to change the
diagnosis and could lead to unnecessary use of antibiotics and exposure to radiation.
Targeted quality improvement strategies that include the use of clinical champions, implementation
of local clinical pathways based on national guidelines, focused educational delivery, educational

text: ## 6.4 Administration of supplemental oxygen through nasal bubble

metadata.section: Summary of recommendations > 6.4 Administration of supplemental oxygen through nasal bubble

text:
## No recommendation: 
WHO makes no recommendation on the use of nasal bubble CPAP to administer oxygen rather
than standard flow oxygen (SFO) through nasal prongs/face mask/headbox for better clinical
outcomes.
6.4.1 Justification
The GDG observed that the available evidence was based on a single small study, in which the criteria of
the outcomes used had varied definitions that may vary from country to country, and which did not include
any of the critical outcomes of interest. The 1hour of follow-up to assess the need for the escalation
of treatment and/or change in the respiratory rate as outcomes did not provide sufficient evidence to
make a recommendation. Pulse oximetry would have been a more objective way of measuring clinical
improvement in hypoxia, which was not reported in this single study.
The GDG decided not to make a recommendation because of inadequate evidence and knowledge gaps
requiring further research.
6.4.2 Summary of evidence
The systematic review identified only one RCT with a sample size of 72 infants aged less than 12months
who were randomized to 36 in the bubble CPAP arm and 36 in the standard arm. The primary outcomes
measured after 1hour were change in respiratory rate, Silverman–Anderson score and Modified Paediatric
Society of New Zealand Severity Score (193).
The findings from this study were that 14 out of 32 infants in the nasal CPAP group and five out of 35 infants
in the standard care group had changes in respiratory rate ≥10. The mean reduction in respiratory rate was
greater in the CPAP group (mean: 8.0; standard deviation (SD): 6.0 vs mean: 5.1; SD: 4.0; MD: 2.9: 95% CI:
−5.3 to −0.5). Both respiratory severity scores showed greater improvement with CPAP. The Silverman–
Anderson score decreased more in the CPAP group (−0.78; SD: 0.87 vs −0.39; SD: 0.73; MD: −0.19; 95% CI:
−0.76 to −0.12). Similarly, the Modified Pediatric Society of New Zealand Severity Score showed greater
improvement with CPAP (−2.5; SD: 3.0 vs −1.08; SD: 1.300; MD: −1.4; 95% CI: −2.5 to −0.3). There were only
two cases that could not tolerate the bubble CPAP (193).
The GDG made no comment on any other aspects of the administration of supplemental oxygen through
nasal bubble CPAP on the evidence-to-decision framework.
WHO consolidated guidelines for the management of common childhood illness: management of asthma in children and 

6.4.3 Research gaps
A large clinical trial with longer follow-up of patients is required comparing bubble CPAP to humidified
high-flow nasal cannula (HHFNC) as second-line oxygen escalation therapy for infants and children
with acute bronchiolitis where low-flow oxygen therapy is insufficient.

text: ## 6.5 Humidified high-flow oxygen versus standard low-flow oxygen

metadata.section: Summary of recommendations > 6.5 Humidified high-flow oxygen versus standard low-flow oxygen

text:
## therapy 
6.5.1 Background
Oxygen therapy supplementation is a commonly prescribed intervention when caring for hypoxic or
severely ill patients. It often takes the form of standard low-flow oxygen which can deliver up to a maximum
of 6 litres per minute or fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) of approximately 0.45 via nasal cannula or
prongs. In standard low-flow oxygen therapy, FiO2 delivery is directly tied to flow rate, and above 6litres
per minute may lead to nasal mucosal irritation and drying of the passages. Humidified high-flow nasal
cannula (HHFNC) therapy is an oxygen supply system capable of delivering up to 100% humidified and
heated oxygen at a flow rate of up to 60litres per minute. The high-flow system ensures delivery of a
fixed concentration of oxygen and the generation of positive end-expiratory pressure, reduces the work of
breathing and clears the nasopharyngeal dead space.
In clinical practice, HHFNC may be used as an alternative to CPAP systems for apnoea of prematurity and
post extubating (194). Some of the reported advantages of HHFNC over CPAP include less trauma to the
nares, simpler application and making it easier to care for the baby as it gives better access to the baby,
including for skin-to-skin contact and feeding (195). Undesired effects include nasal erosion, tiredness
when used over long periods, bradycardia, desaturation or high carbon dioxide, and, in addition, “rain out”
in the circuit can result in lavage and apnoea (196, 197). Studies have shown HHFNC to be safe as an initial
respiratory management, and it is thought to be of benefit for children with bronchiolitis compared with
standard oxygen therapy or nasal CPAP (198).

metadata.section: Summary of recommendations > therapy

text:
## Recommendation 2: 
In infants and children aged less than 2 years, hospitalized with acute bronchiolitis with
hypoxaemia, HHFNC oxygen is suggested rather than SFO.
Condition recommendation, low certainty of evidence.
In most cases, children with acute bronchiolitis should be started on standard low-flow
oxygen, which is very often effective in resolving the hypoxaemia.
HHFNC oxygen is indicated where, despite standard low-flow oxygen therapy, the infant
has persisting hypoxaemia (SpO2 <90%) or severe respiratory distress.
Recommendations for the management of bronchiolitis in infants and young children

6.5.2 Justification
The recommendation in favour of HHFNC was driven by the moderate certainty of evidence of benefit for
the resolution of symptoms/signs such as respiratory rate, heart rate and oxygen saturation, which the
GDG considered to be critical outcomes. The GDG also considered the reduction of 0.85 of a day of length
of stay in ICU as a clinically important outcome in a situation of a peak RSV epidemic, when there are often
too many infants that need hospitalization, as this may save the lives of those who are waiting for hospital
beds. Consequently, the GDG issued a conditional recommendation for high-flow oxygen rather than SFO.
However, the GDG also noted that if the patients started on SFO have responded well, they do not need to
be changed to HHFNC.
6.5.3 Summary of evidence
The systematic review identified seven RCTs comparing HHFNC and SFO conducted in six countries in
Africa, Asia and Europe, with a total of 2197 infants and children with moderate to severe bronchiolitis
(198-204). The HHFNC studies titrated the fraction of inspired oxygen used to maintain oxygen saturation
in a pre-specified range, and the SFO used a variety of delivery methods including nasal prongs, face masks
and headbox oxygen. All seven studies reported on length of hospital stay and resolution of symptoms,
five studies on escalation to the ICU (199, 201-204), and only three studies reported on adverse events
(201-203). Although all were RCTs, all studies had some bias driven by lack of masking/blinding to the
intervention, and some had crossovers from the SFO to the HHFNC arms due to treatment failure.
The mean length of stay in hospital was lower in infants that received HHFNC compared to SFO (weighted
mean difference (WMD): −0.40 days; 95% CI: −1.071 to 0.27; low-certainty evidence), but this finding was
not statistically significant. Two studies reported on length of stay in the ICU; the mean length of stay in
the ICU was lower among infants who received HHFNC compared to the standard of care, which was SFO
(WMD: −0.85days; 95% CI: −2.39 to 0.69); however, this finding was not statistically significant (200, 202). In

on HHFNC, two infants on SFO) (201-203). When “any adverse event” in the two trial arms were compared,
infants that received the HHFNC intervention experienced 57.9% (11 out of 19 infants) adverse events
compared to 42.1% (8 out of 19 infants) among those who were administered SFO (201-203).
Overall, there was moderate certainty of evidence of higher treatment success among those receiving
HHFNC therapy, and moderate certainty of evidence of the length of stay in ICU and escalation to ICU for
further respiratory support, but low certainty of evidence the same length of stay in hospital. There is no
evidence to suggest HHFNC brings about substantially more adverse events than SFO.

of evidence of higher treatment success among those receiving HFNC therapy compared to standard low-
flow oxygen therapy. There was little impact on the duration of hospital stay, or on the length of stay in ICU
and escalation of treatment.
The GDG determined that the undesirable effects were small given that there was no serious adverse
events recorded when compared to standard low-flow oxygen therapy. Adverse events reported included
apnoea, epistaxis, inhaled condensation, oxygen desaturation, oxygen tube disconnection, pneumothorax
and transient bradycardia. There were no differences between HHFNC and SFO therapy in terms of the
incidence of adverse events: 57.9% in the HHFNC group compared to 42.1% in the SFO group.

apnoea, epistaxis, inhaled condensation, oxygen desaturation, oxygen tube disconnection, pneumothorax
and transient bradycardia. There were no differences between HHFNC and SFO therapy in terms of the

Preferences, values and acceptability: The GDG observed that patients and their caregivers will value the
main outcomes that are being measured, and, therefore, decided on probably no important uncertainty
or variability. Stakeholders, including caregivers and clinicians, are more likely to look at the outcome as
acceptable.
Resources required: There was no systematic analysis on the resources required. However, the GDG
considered the possible direct costs as more oxygen therapy is required with HHFNC, along with medical
devices and overhead costs. However, in one study, HHFNC was found to be cost-effective compared to
oxygen by nasal cannula in an infant with bronchiolitis (206).
Equity: The GDG determined that the recommendation will probably increase equity if it is rolled out as a
programme.
Feasibility: Additional considerations that the GDG recognized as influencing feasibility include limited
financial and human resources in some settings that may hinder the implementation of the intervention.
The evidence from contexts and settings where the intervention has been widely deployed suggests that
a comprehensive implementation process and a robust therapy protocol need to be integral to initiating
and managing HHFNC in all hospital locations, including appropriate patient selection and staff education
(207). This intervention requires increased resource requirements, financial requirements, and retraining
health care workers. These factors may limit the feasibility of implementation in some LMIC settings.
6.5.4 Implementation considerations
Ensuring high-quality care and patient safety.
Regular assessment and monitoring of patient vitals (breathing frequency, heart rate, SpO2),
device settings (FiO2, flow), respiratory pattern, breath sounds and comfort level with the device
are prerequisites for high-quality care and improved patient safety (207).
A written protocol specifying the clinical indications and contraindications to guide the initiation
and management of patients while on HHFNC therapy should be in place.
Staff should be trained on the HHFNC protocol, the device, appropriate flow rates according to
weight and age, and on regular monitoring of patients.

## 6.6 Nebulized hypertonic (3%) saline versus no hypertonic saline 
6.6.1 Background
Bronchiolitis is caused by a viral infection and often leads to hospitalization due to respiratory distress.
Bronchiolitis occurs because of the inflammation of the lining of the epithelial cells of the small airways in
the lungs causing mucus production, inflammation and cellular necrosis of these cells. It is the inflammation
of these cells that can obstruct the airway and, ultimately, result in wheezing. Treatment primarily focuses
on supportive care, as there are limited effective pharmacological therapies.
Hypertonic saline (a strong or highly concentrated, usually ≥3%, sterile saltwater solution) breathed in as
a fine mist using a nebulizer may help relieve wheezing and breathing difficulty (208). It is thought to work
by reducing airway oedema through osmotic effects, enhancing mucociliary clearance and rehydrating
airway surfaces (209). However, studies do not consistently provide evidence for a clear long-term benefit
of using nebulized hypertonic saline.

metadata.section: Summary of recommendations > 6.6 Nebulized hypertonic (3%) saline versus no hypertonic saline

text:
## Recommendation 3: 
In infants and children aged less than 2 years presenting or hospitalized with bronchiolitis, a
trial of nebulized hypertonic saline (3%) is suggested rather than no nebulization.
Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence.
The majority of studies used a comparison with normal saline which may underestimate
the effect of hypertonic saline.
A trial of nebulized hypertonic saline in an individual patient may aid in clearance of
secretions, but might not always be effective.
Health facilities experience overcrowding during peak RSV season, making any reduction
in the length of hospital stays through the use of nebulized hypertonic saline especially
valuable.
Health care workers should be aware that hypertonic saline can induce bronchoconstriction
and may often require co-administration with bronchodilators.
WHO consolidated guidelines for the management of common childhood illness: management of asthma in children and 

6.6.2 Justification
The recommendation for nebulized hypertonic saline was mainly driven by a modest reduction in the length
of stay among infants hospitalized with acute bronchiolitis, reduction in the risk of hospitalization among
outpatients and emergency department patients, and the earlier resolution of symptoms. A reduction of
hospital stay for even less than 1day was considered clinically significant, particularly in RSV epidemic
situations, although the certainty of the evidence was low to very low for all outcomes, mainly due to
inconsistency and risk of bias. In addition, nebulized hypertonic saline seems to be cost-effective and a
safe treatment in infants with bronchiolitis, with only minor and spontaneously resolved adverse events.
6.6.3 Summary of evidence
A systematic review identified 38 RCTs conducted over 20years in Africa, the Americas, Asia and Europe,
involving a total of 5114 infants and children with bronchiolitis (208). Study sample sizes ranged from
40 to 772, and patients were followed up for 60minutes to 72hours for primary outcomes. All the trials
used nebulized hypertonic saline alone, or in conjunction with bronchodilators as an active intervention,
and nebulized normal (0.9%) saline or standard treatment as a comparator in children under 24months
with acute bronchiolitis. The primary outcome was length of hospital stay for inpatient trials or rate of
hospitalization for the outpatient or emergency department trials. Other study outcomes included were
duration of oxygen therapy, resolution of symptoms and adverse events (208).
Hospitalized infants treated with nebulized hypertonic saline may have a shorter mean length of hospital
stay compared to those treated with nebulized normal (0.9%) saline or standard care (MD: −0.46days; 95%
CI: −0.56 to −0.36, low-certainty evidence). The risk of hospitalization was reduced by 90 per 1000 patients
for nebulized hypertonic saline compared with nebulized normal saline plus salbutamol and was reduced

metadata.section: Summary of recommendations > Recommendation 3:

duration of oxygen therapy, resolution of symptoms and adverse events (208).
Hospitalized infants treated with nebulized hypertonic saline may have a shorter mean length of hospital
stay compared to those treated with nebulized normal (0.9%) saline or standard care (MD: −0.46days; 95%
CI: −0.56 to −0.36, low-certainty evidence). The risk of hospitalization was reduced by 90 per 1000 patients
for nebulized hypertonic saline compared with nebulized normal saline plus salbutamol and was reduced
by 112 when compared to normal saline alone. Infants and children who received hypertonic saline had a
lower number of days to resolution of wheezing (lower by 1.16days), cough (lower by 0.92days), pulmonary
crackles (lower by 1.42days) compared to those who received normal saline (low-certainty evidence). The
13 trials included in the review (2792 infants; 1479 treated with hypertonic saline, of which 416 (28%) were
co-administered with bronchodilators and 1063 (72%) treated with hypertonic saline alone) reported at
least one adverse event, such as worsening cough, agitation, bronchospasm, bradycardia, desaturation,
vomiting and diarrhoea, most of which were mild and resolved spontaneously (low-certainty evidence)
(208).
Overall, nebulized hypertonic saline may modestly reduce the length of stay among infants hospitalized
with acute bronchiolitis and may slightly reduce time to the resolution of symptoms. Treatment with
nebulized hypertonic saline may also reduce the risk of hospitalization among outpatients and emergency
department patients. Nebulized hypertonic saline seems to be a safe treatment in infants with bronchiolitis,
with only minor and spontaneously resolved adverse events. The certainty of the evidence was low to very
low for all outcomes, mainly due to inconsistency and risk of bias.
The GDG judged the desirable effects of nebulized hypertonic (>3%) saline over 0.9% saline as moderate,
driven by a clinically significant reduction in length of hospital stay, and reduced hospitalization and
readmission rates. The GDG noted that that in peak RSV epidemic season, a reduction of hospital stay for
even less than 1day should be considered significant, depending on the setting. In addition, nebulized
hypertonic saline contributed to earlier resolution of wheezing, cough and pulmonary crackles when
compared to the other interventions. The duration of oxygen therapy was also reduced by 15minutes in
the hypertonic saline group, although this was not statistically significant.

The GDG judged the undesirable effects as trivial, and although there were more adverse effects in the
hypertonic saline treatment arm (4.6%; 67 out of 1449 patients) than standard care (2.3%; 30 out of 1291
patients), this difference was not statistically significant. Nebulized hypertonic saline seems to be a safe
treatment in infants with bronchiolitis, with only minor and spontaneously resolved adverse events. In
addition, the GDG noted that the use of hypertonic saline might lead to 13 more adverse events per 1000
children, although the confidence interval ranged from eight fewer children to 64 more children.
Preferences, values and acceptability: There might be variability in how caregivers will value this main
outcome. Nebulization involves placing a mask on the child’s face and this might raise anxiety levels in
some parents; however, most stakeholders will probably accept the intervention.
Resource required: By reducing hospital stay and admission rate, the use of hypertonic saline may be
cost saving and, therefore, the GDG decided that the resources required were negligible. In one study,
the nebulized 3% hypertonic solution was cost-effective in the inpatient treatment of an infant with
bronchiolitis (210).
Equity: Equity is most likely to vary depending on the context, such as the availability of nebulizers/masks,
infrastructure, etc., and patients in rural settings might be disadvantaged. Hypertonic saline may not be
available, even though it is not costly. The supply chain issues for nebulizers/masks and the quality of
nebulizers during epidemics, as well as the education of parents, will affect implementation.
Feasibility: The considerations looked at when assessing the feasibility of implementation included stock-
outs of nebulizers and the quality of nebulizers, but the GDG was of the opinion that implementation was
probably feasible.
6.6.4 Implementation considerations
Caregivers need to be educated and counselled on the value of nebulization.
When recommending the use of hypertonic saline nebulization on a large scale, especially during
bronchiolitis epidemics, availability and stocks need to be addressed.
The rules for discharge from hospital vary by hospital and by country, and even by age of the admitted
infant, meaning that hospital stays for a 3-month-old may be different from those of a 15-month-old.

7. Monitoring and
evaluation 

Monitoring and evaluation will be built into the dissemination and implementation process to provide
data and information on uptake, implementation and impact of this guideline. In collaboration with the
monitoring and evaluation team of the Department of Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Child and Adolescent
Health and Ageing, WHO, the data on country- and regional-level adoption of the recommendations will
be monitored and evaluated in the short-to-medium term in Member States, through the WHO sexual,
reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health policy survey (211). This survey is conducted
every 4years.
Monitoring and evaluation

8. Dissemination,
adaptation, implementation
and update of the guideline 

As this is a global guideline, Member States are expected to adapt the recommendations to their setting,
considering feasibility, resource availability and other considerations at the national and subnational
level. WHO regional and country offices can assist with the adaptation processes. The dissemination and
implementation of this guideline is to be considered by all stakeholders involved in the provision of care
for children and adolescents.
8.1 Derivative products
These recommendations are part of the consolidated evidence for the updates of the Pocket book of hospital
care for children (1) and the Integrated management of childhood illness (IMCI) chart booklet (3), which are
the main derivatives of these recommendations. In addition to these publications, digital adaptation kits,
training manuals, assessment tools and job aids will be updated to provide consistent implementation
guidance.
8.2 Dissemination
An executive summary containing the recommendations, remarks, implementation considerations and
research priorities will be prepared for public dissemination. WHO will also develop derivative tools to aid

8.2 Dissemination
An executive summary containing the recommendations, remarks, implementation considerations and
research priorities will be prepared for public dissemination. WHO will also develop derivative tools to aid
understanding and adaptation of these recommendations to local contexts.
The recommendations and derivative tools will be disseminated through the WHO website, and targeted
webinars, through a broad network of international partners, including WHO regional and country offices,
ministries of health, professional organizations, universities, WHO collaborating centres, other United
Nations agencies and nongovernmental organizations, among others. Updated recommendations are
also routinely disseminated during meetings and scientific conferences attended by WHO representatives.
The executive summary and recommendations from this publication will be translated into the official
United Nations languages for dissemination through the WHO regional and country offices and during
meetings organized by, or attended by, staff of the Department of Sexual, Reproductive, Maternal, Child
and Adolescent Health and Ageing and the Department of Noncommunicable Diseases and Mental
Health, WHO. Technical assistance will be provided to any WHO regional office wanting to translate these
recommendations into any of their languages. In addition, the publication of journal articles presenting the
recommendations and key implementation considerations will be considered in compliance with WHO’s
open access and copyright policies.
To ensure that these recommendations have a positive impact on asthma in children and adolescents and
on bronchiolitis in infants and young children, coordinated action between WHO, other agencies, national
departments of health and other key stakeholders is needed. National and subnational working groups
should assess current national guidelines and protocols and determine whether development of new
guidelines or updating of existing guidelines is required in line with these new WHO recommendations.
WHO staff at the headquarters, regional and country levels, as well as international agency partners
and international professional societies and national professional associations, can support national
stakeholders in developing or revising existing national guidelines or protocols, and optimizing their
implementation.
In the context of humanitarian emergencies, the adaptation of the current recommendations should
consider their integration and alignment with other response strategies. Context-specific tools and toolkits
may be required in addition to standard tools to support the implementation of the recommendation in
humanitarian emergencies.

Dissemination, adaptation, implementation and update of the guideline

8.3 Adaptation
Public child health programmes require supportive policies and health care services that enable the proper
access to quality services and medicines. WHO headquarters will work with WHO regional and country
offices to assist with the introduction, orientation and adaptation processes. For most Member States, an
intensive and resource-heavy adaptation process will not be necessary. All efforts were made to ensure
that, where possible, the recommendations align with accepted clinical decision-making algorithms.
However, even if the adaptation process is not intensive, ministries of health will have to update their
national standard treatment guidelines based on the Pocket book of hospital care for children (1) and the
Integrated management of childhood illness (IMCI) chart booklet (3), update their training curricula and also
develop plans for building capacity for health care workers on the updated clinical algorithms.
8.4 Implementation
There are a number of important implementation considerations that have been highlighted in the
guideline for end-users as they implement these recommendations. These are necessary in order to provide
accessible, high-quality health services for the management of asthma in children and adolescents, and
the management of bronchiolitis in infants and young children. These considerations may assist policy-
makers, clinicians and other stakeholders to better prepare for implementation. Member States and other
end-users need to ensure that the necessary policies, regulations, infrastructure, supplies and skilled and
competent personnel are in place.
Local professional societies and training institutions have an important role in implementation, and an
all-inclusive and participatory process should be encouraged. National health systems must ensure that
supplies of medicines and commodities such as suitable monitoring are available in health care facilities
where services are provided. In settings where a new practice is introduced (or where recommended
practices are changed), additional training and monitoring may be required. In contexts with high rates of
personnel turnover, pre-service training and regular opportunities for ongoing training and competency
assessment are particularly important.
8.4 Updating

# Guideline Development Group 
In accordance with WHO policies and procedures for guideline development, all members of the Guideline
Development Group (GDG) were required to declare any potential conflicts of interest prior to their
involvement. This was done through the completion and electronic submission of the standard WHO
Declaration of Interests (DOI) form.
In addition, all GDG members, methodologists and external reviewers signed confidentiality agreements
to ensure the integrity and impartiality of the guideline development process.
All submitted DOI forms were reviewed by the WHO Secretariat. Any declared interests were assessed
and managed in line with the procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development6 and
WHO’s Declarations of interests for WHO experts.7 Where a declared interest was considered potentially
significant, appropriate measures were taken. These included conditional participation, partial exclusion
from specific discussions or full exclusion from the guideline process, depending on the nature and extent
of the interest.
At the beginning of each GDG meeting, participants were asked to declare any new or updated interests.
In cases where a GDG member had contributed to a study that informed the evidence for a specific
recommendation, that member was recused from the relevant discussions and decision-making, as
documented in the meeting records.

# 1.1 Initial clinical assessment 
## Clinical history 
1.1.1
Obtain a structured clinical history in people with suspected asthma. Specifically,
check for:
• reported wheeze, noisy breathing, cough, breathlessness or chest tightness,
and any variation (for example, worse during the night or early morning, or
seasonal) in these symptoms
• any triggers that make symptoms worse
• a personal or family history of asthma or allergic rhinitis
• symptoms to suggest alternative diagnoses (see the tables on alternative
diagnoses in wheezy children and alternative diagnoses in adults in the BTS/
SIGN British guideline on the management of asthma SIGN 158.) [NICE 2017,
BTS/SIGN 2019, amended BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.1.2
Do not confirm a diagnosis of asthma without a suggestive clinical history and a
supporting objective test. Code as suspected asthma until the diagnosis is
confirmed. [NICE 2017, amended BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.1.3
If the diagnosis of asthma is confirmed, record the basis for this in the person's
medical records, alongside the coded diagnostic entry. [NICE 2017, amended
BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]

## Physical examination 
1.1.4
Examine people with suspected asthma to identify expiratory polyphonic wheeze
and signs of other causes of respiratory symptoms but be aware that even if
examination results are normal, the person may still have asthma. [NICE 2017]

text:
## presentation 
1.1.5
Treat people immediately if they are acutely unwell or highly symptomatic at
presentation, and perform objective tests that may help support a diagnosis of
asthma (for example, eosinophil count, fractional exhaled nitric oxide [FeNO],
spirometry or peak expiratory flow [PEF] before and after bronchodilator) if the
equipment is available. [NICE 2017, amended BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.1.6
If objective tests for asthma cannot be done immediately for people who are
acutely unwell or highly symptomatic at presentation, carry them out when acute
symptoms have been controlled, and advise people to contact their healthcare
professional immediately if they become unwell while waiting to have objective
tests. [NICE 2017, amended BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.1.7
Be aware that the results of spirometry and FeNO tests may be affected in people
who have been treated with inhaled corticosteroids (the test results are more
likely to be normal). [NICE 2017]

## Adults 
See also algorithm A for a summary of objective tests for diagnosing asthma in adults and
young people (aged over 16 years) with a history suggesting asthma.

1.2.1
Measure the blood eosinophil count or fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) level
in adults with a history suggestive of asthma. Diagnose asthma if the eosinophil
count is above the laboratory reference range or the FeNO level is 50 ppb or
more. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.2.2
If asthma is not confirmed by eosinophil count or FeNO level, measure
bronchodilator reversibility (BDR) with spirometry. Diagnose asthma if the FEV1
increase is 12% or more and 200 ml or more from the pre-bronchodilator
measurement (or if the FEV1 increase is 10% or more of the predicted normal
FEV1). [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.2.3
If spirometry is not available or it is delayed, measure peak expiratory flow (PEF)
twice daily for 2 weeks. Diagnose asthma if PEF variability (expressed as
amplitude percentage mean) is 20% or more. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.2.4
If asthma is not confirmed by eosinophil count, FeNO, BDR or PEF variability but
still suspected on clinical grounds, refer for consideration of a bronchial challenge
test. Diagnose asthma if bronchial hyper-responsiveness is present. [BTS/NICE/

See also algorithm B for a summary of objective tests for diagnosing asthma in children
aged 5 to 16 with a history suggesting asthma.

Measure the FeNO level in children with a history suggestive of asthma. Diagnose
asthma if the FeNO level is 35ppb or more. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.2.6
Ifthe FeNOlevel is not raised, or if FeNO testing is not available, measure BDR
with spirometry. Diagnose asthma if the FEV1 increase is 12% or more from

[BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.2.7
If spirometry is not available or it is delayed, measure PEF twice daily for 2 weeks.
Diagnose asthma if PEF variability (expressed as amplitude percentage mean) is
20% or more. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]

text:
# 1.3 Diagnosing asthma in children under 5 
Diagnosis is hard in this age group because it is difficult to do the tests and there are no
good reference standards.
1.3.1
For children under 5 with suspected asthma, treat with inhaled corticosteroids in
line with the recommendations on medicines for initial management in children
under5, and review the child on a regular basis. If they still have symptoms when
they reach 5 years, attempt objective tests (see the section on objective tests for
diagnosing asthma in adults, young people and children aged 5 to 16). [NICE
2017]
1.3.2
If a child is unable to perform objective tests when they are aged 5:
• try doing the tests again every 6 to 12 months until satisfactory results are
obtained
• refer for specialist assessment if the child's asthma is not responding to
treatment. [NICE 2017, BTS/SIGN 2019, amended BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.3.3
Refer to a specialist respiratory paediatrician any preschool child with an
admission to hospital, or 2 or more admissions to an emergency department, with
wheeze in a 12-month period. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]

text:
# 1.4 Diagnosing occupational asthma 
See the BTS clinical statement on occupational asthma.
1.4.1
In people with adult-onset asthma, poorly controlled established asthma, or
reappearance of childhood asthma, check for a possible occupational component
by asking:
• Are symptoms the same, better or worse on days away from work?
• Are symptoms the same, better or worse when on holiday (time away from
work, longer than usual breaks, at weekends or between shifts)?
© NICE 2026. All rights reserved. Subject to Notice of rights (https://www.nice.org.uk/terms-and-
Page 13 of 

Make sure all answers are recorded for later review. [NICE 2017, BTS/SIGN
2019, amended BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.4.2
Refer people with suspected occupational asthma to an occupational asthma
specialist. [NICE 2017]

text:
# 1.5 Monitoring asthma control 
1.5.1
Monitor asthma control at every review. In addition to asking about symptoms,
check:
• time off work or school due to asthma
• amount of reliever inhaler used, including a check of the prescription record
• number of courses of oral corticosteroids
• any admissions to hospital or attendance at an emergency department due
to asthma.
If control is suboptimal, see recommendation 1.6.1 in the section on principles
of pharmacological treatment. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.5.2
Consider using a validated symptom questionnaire (for example, the Asthma
Control Questionnaire, the Asthma Control Test or the Childhood Asthma Control
Test) at any asthma review. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.5.3
Do not use regular peak expiratory flow (PEF) monitoring to assess asthma
control unless there are person-specific reasons for doing so (for example, when
PEF measurement is part of the personalised asthma action plan). [BTS/NICE/
1.5.4
Consider fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) monitoring for adults with asthma:
• at their regular review, and
• before and after changing their asthma therapy. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]

Page 14 of

control.

• evidence reviewM: pulmonary function monitoring in asthma

text:
# 1.6 Principles of pharmacological treatment 
Licensed indications for asthma inhalers vary between different medicines, different doses
and different devices. Not all asthma inhalers are licensed for use in line with the
recommendations in this guideline. See NICE's information on prescribing medicines or
SIGN's information on prescribing licensed medicines out with their marketing
authorisation and refer to the summary of product characteristics for individual products.
1.6.1
Take into account and try to address the possible reasons for uncontrolled
asthma before starting or adjusting medicines for asthma in adults, young people
and children. These may include:
• alternative diagnoses or comorbidities
• suboptimal adherence (see the recommendation on adherence)
• suboptimal inhaler technique
• smoking (active or passive), including vaping using e-cigarettes
• occupational exposures (see the recommendation on checking for possible
occupational asthma).
• psychosocial factors (for example, anxiety and depression, relationships and
social networks)
© NICE 2026. All rights reserved. Subject to Notice of rights (https://www.nice.org.uk/terms-and-
Page 15 of 

• seasonal factors
• environmental factors (for example, air pollution, indoor mould exposure).
[NICE 2017, BTS/SIGN 2019, amended BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.6.2
If possible, check the fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) level when asthma is
uncontrolled. If it is raised this may indicate poor adherence to treatment or the
need for an increased dose of inhaled corticosteroid (ICS). [BTS/NICE/SIGN
2024]
1.6.3
Do not prescribe short-acting beta2 agonists to people of any age with asthma
without a concomitant prescription of an ICS. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.6.4
After starting or adjusting medicines for asthma, review the response to
treatment in 8 to 12 weeks (see the recommendations on monitoring asthma
control). [NICE 2017, amended BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
For a short explanation of why the committee made these 2024 recommendations
and how they might affect practice, see the rationale and impact section on principles
of pharmacological treatment.
Full details of the evidence and the committee's discussion are in evidence reviewP:

text:
## Inhalers 
1.6.5
Base the choice of inhaler(s) for asthma on:
• an assessment of correct technique
• the preference of the person receiving the treatment
• the lowest environmental impact among suitable devices
• the presence of an integral dose counter.
A spacer should usually be prescribed for use with a metered dose inhaler,
© NICE 2026. All rights reserved. Subject to Notice of rights (https://www.nice.org.uk/terms-and-
Page 16 of 

particularly in children. See the patient decision aid on asthma inhalers and
climate change. [BTS/SIGN 2019, amended BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.6.6
Give people with asthma information on their inhaler treatments. This should
include the medicines they contain, how they work, when they should be taken
and the correct technique to use for each device. [BTS/SIGN 2019, amended
BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.6.7
Observe the person using their inhaler device (and spacer if used) to check they
can use it properly:
• at every asthma review, either routine or unscheduled
• at every asthma-related consultation
• when there is deterioration in asthma control
• when the inhaler device is changed
• when the person asks for it to be checked or changed.
If the person is assessed as being unable to use a device properly, find an
alternative. [NICE 2017, BTS/SIGN 2019, amended BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.6.8
If possible, prescribe the same type of device to deliver preventer and reliever
treatments where more than one inhaler is needed. Consider providing an
additional metered dose short-acting beta2 agonist (SABA) inhaler plus spacer for
emergency use for children under 12 years who may be unable to activate a dry
powder inhaler during an acute asthma attack. [BTS/SIGN 2019, amended BTS/
NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.6.9
Encourage people to take their used or expired inhalers to their pharmacy for
disposal. [BTS/SIGN 2019]

text:
## and over 
1.7.1
Offer a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)/formoterol combination inhaler to
be taken as needed for symptom relief (as-needed AIR therapy) to people aged
12 and over with newly diagnosed asthma. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
In November 2025, only certain budesonide/formoterol inhalers were licensed for
as-needed AIR therapy in mild asthma. The use of any other ICS/formoterol
inhalers would therefore be off-label. The current evidence supporting the use of
budesonide/formoterol is based on the use of a dry powder inhaler. See NICE's
information on prescribing medicines or SIGN's information on prescribing
licensed medicines out with their marketing authorisation.
1.7.2
If the person needing asthma treatment presents highly symptomatic (for
example, regular nocturnal waking) or with a severe exacerbation, start treatment
with low-dose MART (maintenance and reliever therapy) in addition to treating
the acute symptoms as indicated (that is, a course of oral corticosteroids may be
needed). Consider stepping down to as-needed AIR therapy using a low-dose
ICS/formoterol inhaler at a later date if their asthma is controlled. [BTS/NICE/

initial management of newly diagnosed asthma in people aged 12 and over.

text:
## Medicine combination and sequencing in people aged 12 and over 
For guidance on dose ranges of inhaled corticosteroids see inhaled corticosteroid doses
for the BTS, NICE and SIGN asthma guideline.
1.7.3
Offer low-dose MART to people aged 12 and over with asthma that is not
controlled on a low-dose ICS/formoterol combination inhaler used only as
needed. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.7.4
Offer moderate-dose MART to people aged 12 and over with asthma that is not
controlled on low-dose MART. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.7.5
For people aged 12 and over with asthma that is not controlled on moderate-dose
MART despite good adherence:
• Check the fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) level if available, and the
blood eosinophil count. If either of these is raised, refer to a specialist in
asthma care.
• If neither FeNO or eosinophil count is raised, consider a trial of either a
leukotriene receptor antagonist (LTRA) or a long-acting muscarinic receptor
antagonist (LAMA) used in addition to moderate-dose MART. Give the
medicine for a trial period of 8 to 12 weeks unless there are side effects. At
the end of the trial:
－ if asthma is controlled, continue the treatment
－ if control has improved but is still inadequate, continue the treatment and
start a trial of the other medicine (LTRA or LAMA)
© NICE 2026. All rights reserved. Subject to Notice of rights (https://www.nice.org.uk/terms-and-
Page 19 of 

－ if control has not improved, stop the LTRA or LAMA and start a trial of the
alternative medicine (LTRA or LAMA). [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
November 2025: Follow the MHRA safety advice on the risk of
neuropsychiatric reactions in people taking montelukast.
1.7.6
Refer people to a specialist in asthma care when asthma is not controlled despite
treatment with moderate-dose MART, and trials of an LTRA and a LAMA. (See the
Accelerated Access Collaborative consensus pathway on the management of
uncontrolled asthma in adults.) [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
they might affect practice, see the rationale and impact section on medicine
combination and sequencing in people aged 12 and over.

text:
## pathways 
These recommendations are for people with uncontrolled asthma who are on the
treatment pathway recommended by previous NICE and BTS/SIGN guidelines.
1.7.7
Change treatment for people with confirmed asthma who are currently using a
short-acting beta2 agonist (SABA) only to a low-dose ICS/formoterol combination
inhaler used as needed (as-needed AIR therapy). [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.7.8
Consider changing treatment to low-dose MART for people with asthma that is
not controlled on:
• regular low-dose ICS plus SABA as needed
• regular low-dose ICS/LABA (long-acting beta2 agonist) combination inhaler
plus SABA as needed
© NICE 2026. All rights reserved. Subject to Notice of rights (https://www.nice.org.uk/terms-and-
Page 20 of 

• regular low-dose ICS and supplementary therapy (LTRA) plus SABA as
needed.
• regular low-dose ICS/LABA combination inhaler and supplementary therapy
(LTRA) plus SABA as needed. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.7.9
Consider changing treatment to moderate-dose MART for people with asthma
that is not controlled on:
• regular moderate-dose ICS plus SABA as needed
• regular moderate-dose ICS/LABA combination inhaler plus SABA as needed
• regular moderate-dose ICS and supplementary therapy (LTRA or LAMA, or
both) plus SABA as needed
• regular moderate-dose ICS/LABA combination inhaler and supplementary
therapy (LTRA or LAMA, or both) plus SABA as needed. [BTS/NICE/SIGN
2024]
1.7.10
When changing from low- or moderate-dose ICS (or ICS/LABA combination
inhaler) plus supplementary therapy to MART, consider whether to stop or
continue the supplementary therapy based on the degree of benefit achieved

text:
# 5 
These recommendations are for children under5 with newly suspected or confirmed
asthma, or with asthma symptoms that are uncontrolled on their current treatment.
See also algorithm E for a summary of the pharmacological management of asthma in
children under 5.
1.9.1
Consider an 8 to12 week trial of twice-daily paediatric low-dose inhaled
corticosteroid (ICS) as maintenance therapy (with a short-acting beta2 agonist
[SABA] for reliever therapy) in children under5 with suspected asthma and:
• symptoms at presentation that indicate the need for maintenance therapy
(for example, interval symptoms in children with another atopic disorder),or
• severe acute episodes of difficulty breathing and wheeze (for example,
requiring hospital admission, or needing 2 or more courses of oral
corticosteroids). [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.9.2
If symptoms do not resolve during the trial period, take the following sequential
steps:
• check inhaler technique and adherence
• check whether there is an environmental source of their symptoms (for
example mould in the home, cold housing, smokers or indoor air pollution)
• review whether an alternative diagnosis is likely.
© NICE 2026. All rights reserved. Subject to Notice of rights (https://www.nice.org.uk/terms-and-
Page 24 of 

If none of these explain the failure to respond to treatment, refer the child to
a specialist in asthma care. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.9.3
Consider stopping ICS and SABA treatment after 8 to 12weeks if symptoms are
resolved. Review the symptoms after a further 3 months. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.9.4
If symptoms resolve during the trial period, but then:
• symptoms recur by the 3-month review, or
• the child has an acute episode requiring systemic corticosteroids or
hospitalisation, restart regular ICS (begin at a paediatric low dose and titrate
up to a paediatric moderate dose if needed) with SABA as needed and
consider a further trial without treatment after reviewing the child within 12
months. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.9.5
If suspected asthma is uncontrolled in children under5 on a paediatric moderate
dose of ICS as maintenance therapy (with SABA as needed), consider a
leukotriene receptor antagonist (LTRA) in addition to the ICS.Give the LTRA for a
trial period of 8 to 12 weeks (unless there are side effects), then stop it if it is
ineffective. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
November 2025: Follow the MHRA safety advice on the risk of neuropsychiatric
reactions in people taking montelukast.
1.9.6
If suspected asthma is uncontrolled in children under5 on a paediatric moderate
dose of ICS as maintenance therapy and a trial of an LTRA has been unsuccessful
or not tolerated, stop the LTRA and refer the child to a specialist in asthma care
for further investigation and management.[BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]

# 1.10 Decreasing maintenance therapy 
1.10.1
At annual review discuss with the person with asthma (or their family or carer, if
appropriate) the potential risks and benefits of decreasing their maintenance
therapy when their asthma has been well controlled on their current maintenance
therapy. [NICE 2017, BTS/SIGN 2019, amended BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.10.2
When decreasing maintenance therapy:
• Stop or reduce dose of medicines in an order that takes into account the
clinical effectiveness when introduced, side effects and the person's
preference.
• Allow at least 8 to 12 weeks before considering a further treatment reduction.
• If considering step-down treatment for people aged 12 and over who are
using low-dose maintenance inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) plus a short-acting
beta2 agonist (SABA) as needed or low-dose MART (maintenance and
reliever therapy), step down to low-dose ICS/formoterol combination inhaler
as needed (as-needed AIR therapy). [NICE 2017, BTS/SIGN 2019, amended
BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.10.3
Agree with the person (or their family or carer if appropriate) how the effects of
decreasing maintenance therapy will be monitored and reviewed, including self-
monitoring and follow-up with a healthcare professional. [NICE 2017]
1.10.4
Review and update the person's asthma action plan when decreasing
maintenance therapy. [NICE 2017]

text:
## Pregnancy 
1.12.1
People with asthma should have an asthma review during early pregnancy and in
the postpartum period. Emphasise the importance and safety of maintaining
good control of asthma during pregnancy and of continuing asthma medicines to
avoid problems for themselves and their baby. [BTS/SIGN 2019]
1.12.2
Advise anyone who is pregnant and who smokes about the dangers for
themselves and their babies and give appropriate support to stop smoking. See
the NICE guideline on tobacco for more information. [BTS/SIGN 2019]
1.12.3
Advise using the following medicines as normal during pregnancy:
• short-acting and long-acting beta2 agonists
• inhaled corticosteroids
• oral theophyllines. [BTS/SIGN 2019]
1.12.4
Offer oral corticosteroids during pregnancy if needed to treat exacerbations of
asthma. Advise that the benefits of treatment with oral corticosteroids outweigh
the risks. [BTS/SIGN 2019, amended BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.12.5
If leukotriene receptor antagonists or long-acting muscarinic receptor antagonists
are needed to achieve asthma control, they should not be stopped during
pregnancy. [BTS/SIGN 2019, amended BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]

# 1.14 Self-management 
1.14.1
For adults, young people and children aged 5 and over with a diagnosis of asthma
(and their families or carers, if appropriate):
• Offer an asthma self-management programme, comprising a documented
personalised action plan and education. In adults, they may be based on
symptoms or peak expiratory flow (or both); symptom-based plans are
usually preferred for children.
• Explain that there are things that can trigger asthma symptoms and
exacerbations, including indoor and outdoor pollution. Include in the
personalised action plan approaches for minimising exposure to air pollution
and any other personal triggers. For more guidance on how to minimise
exposure and the effect of air pollution on health, see the recommendations
on:
－ vulnerable groups in the NICE guideline on air pollution: outdoor air
quality and health
© NICE 2026. All rights reserved. Subject to Notice of rights (https://www.nice.org.uk/terms-and-
Page 28 of 

－ people with asthma, other respiratory conditions or cardiovascular
conditions in the NICE guideline on indoor air quality at home, and
－ smoking in the NICE guideline on tobacco. [NICE 2017, amended 2021;
BTS/SIGN 2019, amended BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.14.2
Review the content of the personalised action plan, and check that the person
understands it, at the following:
• hospital admission, including in virtual wards
• acute consultations in primary care or emergency department
• annual reviews. [BTS/SIGN 2019, amended BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.14.3
Consider an asthma self-management programme, comprising a written
personalised action plan (including approaches to minimising exposure to indoor
and outdoor air pollution) and education, for the families or carers of children
under 5 with suspected or confirmed asthma. [NICE 2017, amended NICE 2021]
1.14.4
For adults (aged 17 and over) who are using an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) in a
single inhaler, offer an increased dose of ICS for 7 days, within a self-
management programme, when asthma control deteriorates. Clearly outline in the
person's asthma action plan how and when to do this, and what to do if
symptoms do not improve.
When increasing ICS treatment:
• consider quadrupling the regular ICS dose
• do not exceed the maximum licensed daily dose. [NICE 2017]
1.14.5
Include advice in self-management programmes on contacting a healthcare
professional for a review if asthma control deteriorates (see the
recommendations on monitoring asthma control). [NICE 2020, amended BTS/

# 1.15 Risk-stratified care 
1.15.1
Consider actively identifying people with asthma who are at risk of poor
outcomes and tailor care to their needs. Risk factors should include:
© NICE 2026. All rights reserved. Subject to Notice of rights (https://www.nice.org.uk/terms-and-
Page 30 of 

• non-adherence to medicines
• over-use of short-acting beta2 agonist (SABA) inhalers (more than 2 inhalers
per year)
• needing 2 or more courses of oral corticosteroids per year
• 2 or more visits to an emergency department or any hospital admission for
asthma. [BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
For a short explanation of why the committee made this recommendation and how it
might affect practice, see the rationale and impact section on risk-stratified care.

text:
# 1.16 Organisation and delivery of care 
1.16.1
In primary care, people with asthma should be reviewed at least annually and
after any exacerbation by a healthcare professional with appropriate training in
asthma management. The review should incorporate a written personalised
action plan. [BTS/SIGN 2019, amended BTS/NICE/SIGN 2024]
1.16.2
Consider telehealthcare as an option for supporting self-management. [BTS/
SIGN 2019]
1.16.3
Consider computerised decision support systems for patient use to support self-
management. [BTS/SIGN 2019]

# Terms used in this guideline 
This section defines terms that have been used in a particular way for this guideline. For
other definitions see the NICE glossary and the Think Local, Act Personal Care and
Support Jargon Buster.
© NICE 2026. All rights reserved. Subject to Notice of rights (https://www.nice.org.uk/terms-and-
Page 31 of

metadata.section: Terms used in this guideline

text:
## AIR therapy 
Anti-inflammatory reliever (AIR) therapy is treatment with a reliever inhaler that contains a
combination of an inhaled corticosteroid and formoterol. When this is used in response to
symptoms without regular maintenance therapy it is called as-needed AIR therapy. In
November 2025 the only products licensed for as-needed AIR therapy contained
budesonide/formoterol.

metadata.section: Terms used in this guideline > AIR therapy

text:
## Asthma control 
Complete control of asthma is defined as no daytime symptoms, no night-time awakening
due to asthma, no asthma attacks, no need for rescue medication, no limitations on
activity including exercise, normal lung function (in practical terms forced expiratory
volume in 1 second [FEV1] and/or peak expiratory flow [PEF] more than 80% predicted or
best), and minimal side effects from treatment.

metadata.section: Terms used in this guideline > Asthma control

text:
## Atopic disorder 
Atopic disorders are allergic conditions including allergic rhinitis (hay fever), atopic
dermatitis (eczema), allergic asthma and other specific and non-specific allergic
conditions such as food allergies.

metadata.section: Terms used in this guideline > Atopic disorder

text:
## Bronchial challenge test 
A test to measure airway responsiveness (bronchial responsiveness). It is performed by
giving small increments of a bronchoconstrictor (most commonly methacholine) and
measuring the FEV1 after each dose until it falls by a predetermined amount (usually 20%
from baseline).

metadata.section: Terms used in this guideline > Bronchial challenge test

text:
## Bronchial hyperresponsiveness 
A measure of how easily bronchospasm can be induced in the airways. It is measured
using a bronchial challenge test.

metadata.section: Terms used in this guideline > Bronchial hyperresponsiveness

text:
## Bronchodilator reversibility 
A measure of the ability to reverse obstruction in the airways using medicines that widen
© NICE 2026. All rights reserved. Subject to Notice of rights (https://www.nice.org.uk/terms-and-
Page 32 of 

the airways (bronchodilators).

metadata.section: Terms used in this guideline > Bronchodilator reversibility

text:
## Eosinophil count 
The number of eosinophils (a type of white blood cell) measured in a blood sample. Their
levels are raised in asthma and other allergic diseases, and less commonly with malignant
diseases, parasite infections, reactions to some medicines, and a small number of rare
diseases.

metadata.section: Terms used in this guideline > Eosinophil count

text:
## FeNO test 
A test that measures the amount of nitric oxide (NO) present on exhalation, usually
expressed in parts per billion.
FEV1
The amount of air that can be forcibly exhaled from the lungs in one second (forced
expiratory volume in one second).

metadata.section: Terms used in this guideline > FeNO test

text:
## Leukotriene receptor antagonist 
A type of oral medicine that blocks cysteinyl leukotrienes, used in the treatment of asthma
and seasonal allergies. Also known as leukotriene modifiers.

metadata.section: Terms used in this guideline > Leukotriene receptor antagonist

text:
### Long-acting beta2 agonist 
A long-acting medicine that acts on beta-receptors in the airway to relax airway smooth
muscle and relieve symptoms of asthma.

metadata.section: Terms used in this guideline > Leukotriene receptor antagonist > Long-acting beta2 agonist

text:
## Long-acting muscarinic receptor antagonist 
A long-acting medicine that acts on muscarinic receptors in the airway to relax airway
smooth muscle and relieve symptoms of asthma.

metadata.section: Terms used in this guideline > Long-acting muscarinic receptor antagonist

text:
## Maintenance and reliever therapy (MART) 
A form of combined ICS plus formoterol treatment in which a single inhaler containing ICS
© NICE 2026. All rights reserved. Subject to Notice of rights (https://www.nice.org.uk/terms-and-
Page 33 of 

and formoterol is used for daily maintenance therapy and the relief of symptoms as
needed. The terms low-dose MART and moderate-dose MART refer to the dosage of the
maintenance component of MART. People using MART do not normally need a SABA.

metadata.section: Terms used in this guideline > Maintenance and reliever therapy (MART)

text:
## Peak expiratory flow (PEF) variability 
PEF is a measure of the maximum speed of expiration, generally expressed in litres per
minute. PEF variability is a measure of the extent to which this varies over time and can be
expressed numerically as amplitude percentage mean. This is calculated by subtracting
the lowest value measured each day from the highest value on the same day, and
averaging this over the number of days on which PEF is measured

metadata.section: Terms used in this guideline > Peak expiratory flow (PEF) variability

text:
## Skin prick testing 
A test that measures the allergic response of an individual to certain specific allergens
when a very small amount of the specific allergen is introduced into the skin (usually the
inner forearm).

metadata.section: Terms used in this guideline > Skin prick testing

text:
## Specialist in asthma care 
A healthcare professional with higher training in respiratory medicine and proficiency in
the management of asthma. In the context of this guideline, this requires both the relevant
expertise and access to the resources that enable delivery of the diagnostic and
management pathways described in the recommendations.

metadata.section: Terms used in this guideline > Specialist in asthma care

text:
## Uncontrolled asthma 
A term used when asthma is having an impact on a person's lifestyle, or is restricting their
normal activities, because of symptoms such as coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath
and chest tightness. Uncontrolled asthma can include one or both of:
• any asthma exacerbation needing treatment with oral corticosteroids
• frequent regular symptoms such as:
－ needing a reliever inhaler 3 or more days per week, or
－ having 1 or more nights per week when asthma causes night-time waking.
© NICE 2026. All rights reserved. Subject to Notice of rights (https://www.nice.org.uk/terms-and-
Page 34 of 

These can be quantified by questionnaires such as the Asthma Control Questionnaire or
Asthma Control test.
© NICE 2026. All rights reserved. Subject to Notice of rights (https://www.nice.org.uk/terms-and-
Page 35 of
